```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(readr); library(dplyr)
art <- here::here("SciRep_cognitive_impairment_cerebrovascular_events_Shi_2026")
rd  <- function(p) read_csv(file.path(art, p), show_col_types = FALSE, progress = FALSE)
f   <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(round(x, d), format = "f", digits = d)
# numbers as the paper reports them (data/raw/) and the checks on them (R/02_consistency_checks.R)
t1  <- rd("data/raw/table1_baseline.csv")
T1  <- function(v, w) t1[[w]][t1$variable == v]
age_gap <- T1("Age", "ci_med") - T1("Age", "nci_med")
t2  <- rd("data/raw/table2_cox.csv")
T2  <- function(o, g, w) t2[[w]][t2$outcome == o & t2$group == g]
tx  <- rd("data/raw/text_numbers.csv")
TX  <- function(q) as.numeric(tx$value[tx$quantity == q])
cE  <- rd("output/tables/consistency_E_fig2_at_risk.csv")
cEc <- rd("output/tables/consistency_E_fig2_ci_curves.csv")
cF  <- rd("output/tables/consistency_F_timeline.csv")
cG  <- rd("output/tables/consistency_G_screening_epv.csv")
occ <- rd("output/tables/consistency_H_s1_pvalues_denominators.csv") |> filter(variable == "manual worker")
dth <- function(g, w) cE[[w]][cE$panel == "C" & cE$group == g]
# the re-analysis: one row of the stage 3 and stage 4 table (R/03_postprocess.R); stops unless exactly one row matches
sbs <- rd("output/tables/stage4_side_by_side.csv")
m_  <- function(col, v) if (is.null(v)) rep(TRUE, length(col)) else (!is.na(col) & col == v)
R4  <- function(run, quantity, outcome = NULL, group = NULL, time = NULL, period = NULL, rule = NULL) {
  r <- sbs[sbs$run == run & sbs$quantity == quantity & m_(sbs$outcome, outcome) & m_(sbs$group, group) &
           m_(sbs$time, time) & m_(sbs$period, period) & m_(sbs$rule, rule), ]
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1)
  r
}
# central estimate (from a to b); k rescales (100 = per 100 people)
pl  <- function(r, d = 1, k = 1) sprintf("%s (from %s to %s)", f(k * r$stage4_median, d), f(k * r$stage4_lo, d), f(k * r$stage4_hi, d))
md  <- function(r, d = 1, k = 1) f(k * r$stage4_median, d)
HRA <- "HR at given age and sex"
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This page explains, without statistics, what the [technical review](review.qmd) of Shi and
colleagues (Scientific Reports, 2026) found. The review is the reference; this page is a guide to it.
The authors were contacted on 2026-11-20; a reply, if one arrives, is published with the review.
:::

## What the study did

The study follows `{r} f(TX("analysed"), 0)` adults from a community in northern China, aged 40 or
older, who had never had a stroke. Each took the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) once: a
30-point bedside test of memory, orientation and attention. The `{r} f(TX("n_ci"), 0)` people
(`{r} f(TX("pct_ci"), 0)` %) who scored below 24 were called cognitively impaired. Everyone was then
followed for about four years, and first strokes and deaths were counted.

A first ischaemic stroke (the kind caused by a blocked vessel) occurred in
`{r} T2("ischemic stroke", "CI", "events")` of the `{r} f(TX("n_ci"), 0)` people with a low score
(`{r} f(T2("ischemic stroke", "CI", "pct"), 1)` %) and in `{r} T2("ischemic stroke", "NCI", "events")` of the
`{r} f(TX("n_nci"), 0)` others (`{r} f(T2("ischemic stroke", "NCI", "pct"), 1)` %). After taking age, sex,
schooling and a few vascular measures into account, the authors report that a low score went with
about two and a half times the rate of stroke. They conclude that cognitive impairment
"independently forecasted" stroke, and that "cognitive screening could be valuable for identifying
stroke-free adults who are at a greater risk".

## What we did

We read the paper against a fixed checklist and recomputed every number that can be recomputed
from its tables and figures. The authors' data are not public, so we rebuilt a dataset consistent
with everything the paper prints: the counts of events, the numbers of people still followed at
each year, the ages of the two groups. On it we repeated the authors' analysis and then asked two
questions the paper does not ask. How much of the difference between the groups is left when two
people of the same age are compared? And how many of the people who later had a stroke would the
test have picked out? All of this is code in a public repository, and the authors have been asked
for the original data so that the same code can be run on them.

## What we found, area by area

The checklist looks at six areas. The table counts the problems recorded in each; the technical
review lists every one of them with its evidence.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-quality-plain
#| tbl-cap: "Problems found, by area. A problem is 'settled by the paper's own numbers' when no assumption and no extra data are needed to see it; the others depend on a stated assumption or on the original data. 'Serious' means it affects a conclusion of the paper."
source(here::here("lib/quality_table.R"))
plain_area <- c("Design" = "How the study was set up", "Measurement" = "What was measured, and how",
                "Model adequacy" = "How the data were analysed",
                "Internal consistency" = "Whether the numbers agree with each other",
                "Reporting" = "How it was reported", "Inference" = "What was concluded")
plain_rating <- c("conclusions at risk" = "puts the conclusions at risk", "major concerns" = "serious",
                  "minor concerns" = "minor", "no concern found" = "none found")
quality_table("P002") |>
  transmute(Area = unname(plain_area[Domain]),
            `Problems found` = Critical + Major + Minor,
            `Of which serious` = Critical + Major,
            `Settled by the paper's own numbers` = Confirmed,
            `Our reading` = unname(plain_rating[Rating])) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe", align = "lrrrl")
```

## Five things a reader should know

**1. The test misses most of the people who went on to have a stroke.** Of the
`{r} T2("ischemic stroke", "overall", "events")` people who had a first ischaemic stroke,
`{r} T2("ischemic stroke", "CI", "events")` had a low score. The other
`{r} T2("ischemic stroke", "NCI", "events")` had a normal one. A screening test is judged by how many
future cases it picks out, and this one picks out
`{r} f(100 * cG$sensitivity[cG$outcome == "ischemic stroke"], 0)` in every 100. Seen from the other side, of
100 people with a low score, about `{r} f(100 * cG$ppv[cG$outcome == "ischemic stroke"], 0)` had a stroke in
the following years. The paper recommends screening without giving either number; both follow
from its own table.

**2. The two groups differ in age by `{r} f(age_gap, 1)` years.** The people with a low score had a
median age of `{r} f(T1("Age", "ci_med"), 1)`, the others `{r} f(T1("Age", "nci_med"), 1)`. Stroke becomes more common
with every year of age, so an older group has more strokes whatever its test scores. The paper
corrects for age, but does not say how much it found age to matter, and the corrected result
depends on exactly that. If each ten years of age multiply the stroke rate by about one and a half,
the paper's corrected figure follows. If they double it, as is often reported for stroke, most of
the difference between the groups is age, and what is left could be nothing.

**3. A low score partly measures schooling.** Of the `{r} f(TX("n_ci"), 0)` people called impaired,
`{r} T1("Education: illiteracy/primary school", "ci_n")`
(`{r} f(T1("Education: illiteracy/primary school", "ci_pct"), 0)` %) had primary schooling or none, against
`{r} f(T1("Education: illiteracy/primary school", "nci_pct"), 0)` % of the others. The MMSE asks people
to read, write, count backwards and copy a drawing, and people with little schooling score lower on
it without being ill. One cut-off was used for everyone. Some of those labelled "cognitively
impaired" may simply have left school early.

**4. The main figure and the main table cannot come from the same data.** The paper's figure shows,
for the low-score group, a curve that climbs in `{r} cEc$n_steps[1]` equal steps to
`{r} f(cEc$final_value[1], 0)`, the top of the axis: the picture of `{r} cEc$n_steps[1]` people who all had
a stroke. The
table says `{r} T2("ischemic stroke", "CI", "events")` of `{r} f(TX("n_ci"), 0)` did. The numbers printed
under the same figure agree with the table, not with the curve. This is a statement about the
numbers, not about anyone's intentions; a figure drawn from a different file would produce it.

**5. The dates do not add up.** The test was given in 2012 or 2013 and the follow-up ended on the
last day of 2015. That leaves between `{r} f(cF$min_follow_up[1], 0)` and
`{r} f(cF$max_follow_up[1], 0)` years, yet the paper reports that half the participants were followed
for more than `{r} f(TX("median_follow_up"), 1)` years. Follow-up of that length fits a start in
2010 or 2011, when the cohort was recruited, which is two years before the test was given. And by
the paper's own counts of people still followed, at least
`{r} dth("NCI", "min_events_after_y4")` of the `{r} dth("NCI", "events_total")` deaths in the larger group
happened after the fourth year, on a time axis that ends a few weeks later. Deaths do not usually
arrive all at once. Only the original records can say what happened here.

There is a sixth point for readers who look at the headline number. It comes from an analysis that
includes the participants' occupation, and occupation was recorded for only about
`{r} f(100 * occ$inc_den_lo / TX("analysed"), 0)` % of them. The headline result is therefore based on
fewer people and fewer strokes than the table suggests, and the paper does not say how many.

## What our re-analysis shows

Everything in this section rests on a dataset rebuilt from the paper's tables and figures, not on
the original records. The numbers in brackets are the range we are fairly confident the true value
lies in.

- **Before any correction, the low-score group had strokes about four times as often.** Our figure
  is `{r} pl(R4("isch", "HR", "ischemic stroke"))` times the rate of the other group. This is the
  one result that the paper's counts clearly support. It compares an older group with a younger one.
- **In absolute terms the difference is about `{r} md(R4("isch_early_split", "RD", "ischemic stroke", time = 4.2), 0, 100)` people in a hundred.** Of 100 people with a low
  score, about `{r} md(R4("isch_early_split", "F", "ischemic stroke", group = "CI", time = 4.2), 0, 100)` had a
  first ischaemic stroke in four years; of 100 with a normal score, about `{r} md(R4("isch_early_split", "F", "ischemic stroke", group = "NCI", time = 4.2), 0, 100)`. The paper
  describes this as "a 2.32 to 2.55 times higher risk", which mixes up two different kinds of
  number; the risks themselves are these.
- **At the same age, the answer depends on how much age matters.** Comparing two people of the same
  age and sex, one with a low score and one without, the stroke rate of the first is
  `{r} pl(R4("isch_P1", HRA))` times that of the second if ten years of age multiply the rate by about
  one and a half; `{r} pl(R4("isch_P2", HRA))` times if they double it; and
  `{r} pl(R4("isch_P3", HRA))` times if we admit we do not know. A value of 1 means no difference.
  Only the first range excludes it.
- **A birthday does better than the test.** In our rebuilt population the rule "aged 65 or older"
  picks out about `{r} md(R4("isch_P2", "sensitivity", rule = "age >= 65"), 0, 100)` of every 100 people who
  will have a stroke; the low test score picks out `{r} f(100 * cG$sensitivity[cG$outcome == "ischemic stroke"], 0)`. Adding the test to age and sex barely
  changes how well people can be ranked by their risk.
- **A low score is worth a few years of age, perhaps none.** Under the doubling assumption, a
  low score carries the same extra stroke rate as being about
  `{r} md(R4("isch_P2", "age-equivalent, years"), 0)` years older, with a range from
  `{r} f(R4("isch_P2", "age-equivalent, years")$stage4_lo, 0)` to
  `{r} f(R4("isch_P2", "age-equivalent, years")$stage4_hi, 0)` years.

### The numbers side by side

The same results as a table. The paper's numbers are as printed; ours are the central estimate
with its range. The technical review has the full version, with what each quantity is.

| What is compared | The paper's number | Our number | In plain words |
|:----------|:--------|:--------|:--------------|
| Stroke rate, low score against normal score, no correction | `{r} f(T2("ischemic stroke", "CI", "hr_unadj"))` times | `{r} pl(R4("isch", "HR", "ischemic stroke"))` times | About four times as often, in a group `{r} f(age_gap, 1)` years older |
| The same, at equal age and sex | `{r} f(T2("ischemic stroke", "CI", "hr_m1"))` times (from `{r} f(T2("ischemic stroke", "CI", "hr_m1_lo"))` to `{r} f(T2("ischemic stroke", "CI", "hr_m1_hi"))`), also corrected for schooling | `{r} pl(R4("isch_P1", HRA))` if age matters moderately; `{r} pl(R4("isch_P2", HRA))` if it doubles the rate each decade | Somewhere between no difference and three to four times; the paper's figure is one point in that range |
| People per 100 with a first ischaemic stroke in four years | `{r} f(T2("ischemic stroke", "CI", "pct"), 1)` and `{r} f(T2("ischemic stroke", "NCI", "pct"), 1)` in the table; a curve reaching the top of the axis in the figure | `{r} pl(R4("isch_early_split", "F", "ischemic stroke", group = "CI", time = 4.2), 1, 100)` and `{r} pl(R4("isch_early_split", "F", "ischemic stroke", group = "NCI", time = 4.2), 1, 100)` | About seven in a hundred against two, close to the table; the figure disagrees with both |
| Future strokes picked out by the test | not reported; screening recommended | `{r} T2("ischemic stroke", "CI", "events")` of `{r} T2("ischemic stroke", "overall", "events")`, or `{r} f(100 * cG$sensitivity[cG$outcome == "ischemic stroke"], 0)` in 100 | More than four in five future strokes are missed |
| Future strokes picked out by "aged 65 or older" | not considered | about `{r} md(R4("isch_P2", "sensitivity", rule = "age >= 65"), 0, 100)` in 100 | Age alone finds more of them than the test |

## What this does and does not mean

It does not mean that memory and stroke are unrelated. Damage to small vessels in the brain can
lower a test score years before it causes a stroke, and the earlier studies that the paper cites
found a modest link (a stroke rate about `{r} f(TX("meta_analysis_hr"))` times as high).

It means that this paper, as published, shows that an older and less schooled group had more
strokes, and does not show how much of that is left once age is properly accounted for. Its
recommendation to screen has no number behind it, and the numbers in its own table speak against
it. Its main figure and its dates disagree with its tables in ways the authors should be able to
resolve with their data.

The authors received a data request and
notice of this commentary before anything was published. If they share their data, the same code
runs on them and this page is updated.
